title: OSCS: Online Selection with Provable FAR Control for LLM Safety
claim: Our online selection method keeps the empirical error rate below the user-specified target level across time and diverse attack settings.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared legend on top, red dashed target line
description: A single row of four line plots, one for each backdoor attack: BadNets, AddSent, StyleBkd and SynBkd. Each plot has time step on the x-axis, from 0 to 20000. The y-axis is empirical FAR, from 0.00 to 0.08. A shared legend at the top lists MDS (blue solid line), BadActs (orange solid line) and Target FAR Level (red dashed horizontal line at 0.05). Each curve has a light shaded band for variability. The curves start with a brief spike or noisy transient early on, then settle into stable plateaus between about 0.02 and 0.047. Every plateau stays below the red target line. The eye goes first to the red dashed threshold and then to the curves converging beneath it. Bold attack names sit below each panel.
caption: The FAR control performance of OSCS over time. X-axis represents the time step and Y-axis represents the empirical FAR up to
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to malicious inputs, posing serious risks in high-stakes applications. Although existing detection-based defenses achieve strong empirical performance, they generally lack explicit control over the false acceptance rate (FAR), a critical safety requirement in sensitive deployment scenarios. This challenge is further complicated by two practical constraints: the lack of malicious calibration samples and the streaming nature of real-world inputs. To address these challenges, we propose \textit{OSCS}, a novel framework for online FAR control without requiring malicious calibration data. OSCS leverages detection scores produced by existing defenses and employs recursive density estimation to estimate benign probability from the test stream. Based on these estimates, OSCS performs real-time accept/reject decisions while provably satisfying a user-specified FAR target. Theoretically, we show that OSCS controls the FAR up to a vanishing excess term under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments on backdoor and jailbreak attack tasks further demonstrate the effectiveness of OSCS, showing that it consistently achieves robust FAR control across diverse attack settings while outperforming existing baselines.
